global-economics-93e64a748a.headline: Amazon shares fall 6% as $77 billion AI spending raises cash flow concerns
global-economics-93e64a748a.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-93e64a748a.fulltext:
Updated - October 30, 2026  at 05:46 AM.
Amazon.com Inc. shares dropped after the company reported greater capital spending than anticipated and the slowest growth in the core e-commerce business in three years.
Amazon said it spent more than $77 billion on property and equipment in the third quarter, far more than analysts’ estimates, while pursuing its effort to build data centers and fulfill demand for artificial intelligence services.
Sales in the holiday period will be $240 billion to $247 billion, the company said Thursday in a statement. Analysts were looking for $244.5 billion. Third-quarter revenue was also a little lower than anticipated, rising 12% to $201.9 billion.
The company’s spending led to a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months.
Revenue at the cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, accelerated for the sixth straight quarter, contrasting with signs of sluggish growth in the company’s core businesses. Online sales gained just 2% to $68.5 billion, the lowest increase since early 2023, when Amazon was still working through the post-pandemic slump in online retail. Advertising sales, a business closely tied to the e-commerce franchise, rose 11%, the slowest rate since Amazon began breaking out such results in 2020.
John Tomlinson, an analyst with research firm M Science, said some of the relative weakness in retail is likely the result of Amazon’s decision to move its Prime Day sales to June this year, from July. Still ,“there’s a little bit of a crack in the armor here,” he said. “There’s a lot of focus on how much companies are spending on AI.”
The AWS business has picked up this year, fueled by sales to artificial intelligence companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which both rely in part on Amazon servers to power their models. Amazon has also added to its fleet of data centers, boosting its ability to provide computing power to businesses.
Chief Executive Officer Andy Jassy said the company’s cloud business was also showing strength beyond AI. The core AWS computing power and storage rental business grew at “their fastest rates in several years,” he said on a conference call with analysts.
The company said in July that it would likely spend $220 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, up from a prior forecast as a crunch in memory chips curbed supply. Amazon stuck to that forecast on Thursday.
The shares fell about 6% in extended trading after closing at $243.79 in New York. The stock had gained 5.6% this year through Thursday’s close.
“AWS’s accelerating growth fell short of overblown expectations and the higher competitive bar set by Microsoft and Google,” said Sky Canaves, an analyst with Emarketer. “The cloud unit’s improving operating margin was one welcome signal, but it may not be sufficient to alleviate concerns about the sharp spike in capex spending and corresponding freefall of its free cash flow.”
Investors’ disappointment with Amazon’s results is similar to the reaction to rival Alphabet Inc.’s report on Wednesday. Alphabet reported search and advertising sales that reinforced investor concerns about AI’s threat to its core business, sending its shares down 13% at the close Thursday — the worst day ever for the stock. Also Wednesday, Microsoft Corp. reported a 48% gain in cloud revenue while keeping its capital expenditures in check, soothing investors concerned about lavish spending on AI. Microsoft shares fell less than 1% on Thursday.
Canaves said the Prime Day schedule move “doesn’t fully explain the weakness in online stores and advertising growth, suggesting that consumer pressure may be becoming more visible as shoppers pull back where they can, and this has a knock-on effect on advertisers’ willingness to spend.”
Third-quarter operating income increased to $17.8 billion, compared with $11.4 billion in the period a year ago. Amazon projected profit in the holiday quarter of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion. Analysts, on average, estimated $33 billion.

deep-tech-1deb7ef615.headline: Japan explores using Indian firing ranges to test long-range missiles and drones
deep-tech-1deb7ef615.fulltext:
Japanese army chief General Masayoshi Arai has said that officials are visiting India to explore the possibility of using the country's firing ranges to test missiles and attack drones. Japan has already entered into a similar agreement with Australia.
A Japanese military's Type 88 surface-to-ship missile launcher fires during the Joint Task Force (JTF) Maritime Strike, part of Balikatan, the annual joint military exercises between the United States and the Philippines, at Culili Point Sand Dunes, Paoay, Ilocos, Norte province. (Photo: Noel Celis/Reuters)
Japanese army chief General Masayoshi Arai on Tuesday said officials were visiting India to examine the possibility of using the country's firing ranges to test missiles and drones, according to The Japan Times.
Arai said officials were searching for a range to test the 1,000-kilometre-range Type 24 missile and smaller attack drones. They have been dispatched to India as part of efforts to determine how to conduct training that makes full use of the missile's 1,000-kilometre range, which he described as "a major challenge".
"We are currently examining this issue, including how to secure training environments domestically and, if necessary, how to utilise training environments overseas," said Arai.
The search is part of Japan's broader efforts to build a multilayered coastal defence system incorporating large numbers of inexpensive unmanned aerial, surface, and underwater vehicles for both reconnaissance and attack missions alongside standoff missiles capable of striking targets from beyond an enemy's range.
The Japan Times reported that testing these platforms in Japan as part of the 'Synchronised, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense' (Shield) drone system faces several challenges, such as the impact of radio frequencies and drone communications on civilian televisions and smartphones as well as friction with local governments over testing activities.
The efforts are part of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to strengthen Japan's security preparedness, advance the country's military industry, and expand defence partnerships with like-minded nations. The aim is to safeguard Japan and the wider region amid rising Chinese aggression in the Indo-Pacific and North Korea's expansion and modernisation of its missile arsenal.
Japan has already entered into a similar arrangement with Australia to test munitions. Japan, India, and Australia are members of the Quad and also cooperate under the trilateral 'JAI' framework. The grouping has gained greater significance during US President Donald Trump's second term as he has withdrawn from the Indo-Pacific as part of his pivot towards China.

deep-tech-c9a53b7784.headline: Chinese AI chipmaker Iluvatar CoreX says new GPU matches Nvidia’s H200 as chip gap closes
deep-tech-c9a53b7784.fulltext:
Search the way you think. Try our AI-powered search to find news faster.
South Korea’s chip giants ride record AI windfall, but can China catch up?
Chinese artificial intelligence chipmaker Iluvatar CoreX claims that its new Tiangai 300 graphics processing unit (GPU) can match and even surpass Nvidia’s H200 in real-world AI workloads, highlighting efforts by domestic players to close the technology gap with the US chip giant.
In a live demonstration for mainland Chinese media outlets on Wednesday, the Shanghai-based firm showed the Tiangai 300 outperforming the H200 in complex multimodal tasks, including text-to-image and text-to-video generation using frontier AI models such as Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, according to a report by Chinese tech media outlet Xinzhixun.
The H200 is the most advanced Nvidia AI processor approved for export to China under current US trade rules.
In one text-to-image test, the Tiangai 300 achieved a 100 per cent completion rate with a throughput of 0.101 images per second, compared with the H200’s 87.5 per cent success rate and 0.086 images per second, although the Chinese chip took 0.64 seconds longer to complete the task, Xinzhixun reported.
The demonstration corroborated findings from earlier third-party benchmark tests conducted by state-backed Shanghai INESA. Those tests showed the Tiangai 300, unveiled in July, reaching 1.05 times the throughput of the H200 “under typical deployment conditions”.
That made it the first Chinese general-purpose GPU to match the US processor in empirical testing, the report said.
A separate report by Chinese financial outlet Wallstreetcn on Thursday noted that the Tiangai 300 beat the H200 in mixture-of-experts (MoE) throughput by 15 per cent, while slashing first-token latency by up to 30 per cent in long-text processing. MoE is an architecture that routes tasks to specialised sub-networks to save computing power.
In AI, training is the resource-intensive process of teaching a model to learn from vast data sets, while inference is the subsequent stage of putting that trained model to work answering live user prompts.
On the AI training front, the Tiangai 300 delivered 1.33 times the effective throughput of Nvidia’s prior-generation H100 when fine-tuning Alibaba Group Holding’s open-source Qwen3-32B model, the report added. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Iluvatar did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.
The performance claims come as China’s top GPU contenders – including Iluvatar, Biren Technology, MetaX Integrated Circuits, Enflame Technology and Moore Threads – are racing to deliver viable home-grown substitutes under Beijing’s self-sufficiency drive and tightening US trade curbs.
The H200, which Nvidia launched in late 2023, has become a key focal point in Sino-US tech rivalry. While Washington eased conditions earlier this year under a revised licensing framework to permit H200 shipments to China, Beijing has discouraged domestic tech champions from buying foreign chips to bolster the local ecosystem.
Nvidia said in August that it had commenced its first H200 data-centre processor shipments to China under the new US rules, ending an extended supply freeze.
Iluvatar, which went public in Hong Kong earlier this year, has laid out ambitious targets to counter US dominance. In January, the firm unveiled a multi-year architecture road map aiming to leapfrog Nvidia’s advanced Rubin platform within two years.
To prove commercial viability beyond lab tests, Iluvatar said earlier this month that its Tiangai series had reached 10,000-card-scale deployments, giving it crucial experience in system-level delivery and operations maintenance.
The chipmaker is also expanding beyond cloud-connected data centres into edge computing – running AI directly on local machines, vehicles and connected devices.
Iluvatar’s Tongyang TY1200 processor outperformed Nvidia’s Thor T5000 by 20 per cent in specific large language model tests, according to Wallstreetcn.
Ann Cao is a Shanghai-based technology reporter for the Post, covering technology start-ups and policies in the city and eastern China. She graduated from the University of Hong Kong with a master's degree in journalism.

ai-56fa7327f2.headline: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
ai-56fa7327f2.fulltext:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.
Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.
As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.
Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.
AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.
Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company.

global-economics-5ac7099593.fulltext:
European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early
Christine Lagarde will leave the post in February, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde will step down months before her term ends, kicking off a race to succeed her against a turbulent backdrop in the eurozone.
Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will leave the post on February 7, about nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term. She said in a filmed statement posted on X that she was leaving “with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future”.
The move gives European Union leaders time to choose her successor before April’s French presidential election, which polls have suggested far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win.
The timing could allow current European Council members, including French President Emmanuel Macron, to take part in appointing Lagarde’s successor before France’s vote.
Macron, who is not allowed to run again, thanked Lagarde in a post on X for “the determined action she led at the head of the European Central Bank” during “a period marked by numerous crises”.
“The transition at the head of the ECB must now be prepared in an orderly and balanced manner with our European partners,” the leader of the eurozone’s second-largest economy added.
However, Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, warned: “If the impression arises that such a departure is timed around national elections, it damages trust in an institution that must stand above any domestic political calculation.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leader of the eurozone’s largest economy, said Lagarde had led the bank “with great aplomb during challenging times”, and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen thanked Lagarde “for everything you have done for Europe and the euro”.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure praised her tenure. “Christine Lagarde has been an exceptional President of the ECB. As Europe navigated through crises and difficult times, she brilliantly modernised and strengthened the institution,” he posted on social media.
Marcel Fratzscher, president of the German Institute for Economic Research, told the Reuters news agency the early exit gives governments “an opportunity to appoint a successor who will safeguard European values and protect the ECB’s independence”.
Markets appeared unfazed. “Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde and be quite similar, whoever takes over,” Simon Dangoor, head of fixed income macro investing at Goldman Sachs told Reuters.
Lagarde, appointed in October 2019, steered the bank through the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the United States-Israel war on Iran.
The ECB faced criticism for responding too slowly to the 2022 inflation surge, caused by post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks and the war on Ukraine. Inflation is currently running at almost double the bank’s 2 percent target amid worries over France’s public finances.
A former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, Lagarde arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience, prompting some market participants to warn of a “credibility risk”.
In March 2020 as the pandemic shook sovereign debt markets, she said the bank was not there to narrow the gap between Italian and German borrowing costs. She went on to show that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks.
Sources told the AFP news agency that leaving early would give Lagarde “greater freedom to express her views”. She has hinted she could campaign in the French presidential race, saying a European voice was needed in the debate.

A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.
The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.
The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.
But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

deep-tech-8b4a4d972e.fulltext:
How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
KYIV, Ukraine — Like many tech entrepreneurs in Ukraine, Yaroslav Azhnyuk turned to developing drone warfare after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Drones have transformed the way wars are fought. Azhnyuk says artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable.
"When the other side has orders of magnitudes higher capabilities, it gives you an asymmetric advantage," he says. "It can make you 10,000 times more effective."
Azhnyuk runs the Ukraine-based defense firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. They are among the top companies producing AI-powered drones in Ukraine. Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1.
Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine. AI warfare is part of a high-tech arms race that has many worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.
Azhnyuk told NPR that he acknowledges the concern over destructive weapons but says it's not specific to AI.
"It has been with humanity since the invention of fire or steel," he says. "Any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad. And in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool."
Cameras that "fling explosives"
Azhnyuk is 37, a gregarious computer scientist who hails from a family of scholars and scientists. NPR meets him in a conference room in Kyiv; for security reasons he asked us not to reveal much else about the location.
He worked for years in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including Petcube, which makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and even entertain pets while they're alone.
"These cameras allow pet parents to watch pets when they're not at home," he says, "and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. We sold a million of these devices that are quite popular in the U.S."
After Russia launched its full-scale war, Azhnyuk, by then living in Ukraine, pivoted to the defense space.
"I was like, OK, I've got to move on from Petcube and do something to protect my country," he says. "And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats but cameras that fling explosives at people who came to occupy our land."
The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first-person-view or FPV drones.
"We are leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras," he says.
A drone named after a poet
The autonomous Lupynis TFL-1 drone combines a small, affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the last 500 meters (or 0.3 miles) of the flight.
"But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude," he says. "Or even the kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla."
Azhnyuk says this AI technology uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software "which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly toward the target autonomously."
The Fourth Law's autonomous drone is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet and political activist Anatoliy Lupynis, who endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and psychiatric torture. The company named all its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century.
"It is important for us to help to resurrect those people," Azhnyuk says. "Their ideas are still with us. And now they're fighting back."
"The drone is doing everything itself"
The Fourth Law teams test the Lupynis TFL-1 drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a fold-out table near a copse of trees and a hornets' nest.
A slight, sandy-haired man stands up from the fold-out table and says he's the head of the test and integration team. He uses the military call sign Stab. The Fourth Law asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons.
Stab points to a drone.
"So you see here is our camera, plus the microcomputer inside this 3-D model," Stab says. "All of the mind is here," he adds with a laugh.
The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep-learning neural network that uses hours of combat footage to recognize targets.
"Like vehicles, light-armored vehicles, tanks, and flying objects," he says.
The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot, who also asked us to use his call sign, Professor. He navigates the drone with a control stick. He selects a target and checks a video monitor. Then he sees a red flash.
"That means it has locked," Stab says.
The drone has locked onto its target: a dilapidated car an employee is driving along a dirt road. Professor lets go of the control stick. The drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course.
"See, Professor is doing nothing, and the drone is doing everything itself," Stab says.
On the battlefield, the drone would carry an explosive to hit the car. The test drone doesn't have one.
Stab says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam. He also insists safeguards are in place so The Fourth Law drones won't go rogue. Humans select the target, he says.
Survival vs. the ethics of AI
Back in the conference room, Azhnyuk says his company's AI-powered drones are not killer robots.
"They're very far from a Terminator kind of scenario, right?" he says. "These are just sort of calculators. Like they're no more likely for a Terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells."
He does acknowledge, though, that AI is developing quickly. "It's not unthinkable," he says, "to imagine that some years in the future there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions on designating targets or not."
That's the future. Right now he is focused on what Ukraine needs today.
"Our adversaries are using the very same technologies, and if they use AI for decision-making in an offensive scenario, and if we refuse to use AI in decision-making in a defensive scenario, we've lost, right?" he says. "Because their systems are capable of making decisions in microseconds, and human control takes minutes, hours and sometimes days."
If Ukraine loses, he says, "there's no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI."
The most important thing, he says, is don't die.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this story from Kyiv.

climate-energy-7fd13d78b5.fulltext:
Analysis: China’s clean-tech exports in 2026 to avoid as much CO2 as Brazil emits in a year
China’s exports in 2026 of clean-energy technologies, such as solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles, are on track to cut emissions beyond its borders by 2%, reveals new analysis.
This guest post is by:
Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and senior fellow at Asia Society Policy Institute
The impact of these Chinese exports on carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions around the world grew by 26% year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026, having already risen by 36% in 2025.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief is based on detailed data for clean-tech product exports, the electricity system in destination countries and emissions during manufacturing in China.
If the latest trends continue for the rest of the year, then Chinese clean-tech exports in 2026 alone will avoid around 450m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) – roughly equivalent to Brazil’s annual emissions.
Other key findings from the analysis include:
- Electric car and heavy vehicle shipments grew by 61% year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026, wind-turbines by 45%, batteries 39%, solar 22% and electric two-wheelers by 21%.
- Over the lifetime of the equipment, exports in 2026 are on track to avoid 8,400MtCO2, equivalent to the annual emissions of the US and India combined.
- This lifetime avoided emissions total for exports in 2026 is up by a quarter from 6,800MtCO2 in 2025 and up by two-thirds from 5,000MtCO2 in 2024.
- Wind- and solar-equipment exports from China in 2026 will generate as much electricity each year as roughly 100 coal-fired power plants.
- While the majority of clean-tech exports by value went to the global north in the first three quarters of 2026, some 76% of lifetime avoided emissions were in the global south.
- This includes 52% of lifetime avoided emissions being in south and south-east Asia, reflecting solar shipments from China being installed onto high-carbon power grids.
- Chinese-owned clean-energy projects built in other countries doubled from 2022-25, but the amount of CO2 avoided remains small compared to equipment exports.
The analysis shows that most of China’s clean-energy exports have been built on new or expanded markets, enabling other producers to maintain their own sales volumes.
In addition, clean-energy sales within China are larger than exports for most technologies, but a domestic solar slowdown could exacerbate trade tensions, if it continues.
Clean-tech exports
China has become the pre-eminent producer of clean-energy technologies, from solar panels and wind turbines through to batteries and electric vehicles.
The majority of China’s clean-tech production is destined for the domestic market. But it has also become a major exporter – and these exports are avoiding significant amounts of CO2.
Previous analysis for Carbon Brief showed that these clean-energy exports in 2024 would cut emissions in countries outside China by around 1%.
The latest analysis shows that China’s clean-tech exports in 2026 are on track to avoid around 450MtCO2, as shown in the figure below, which is nearly 2% of global emissions outside China. It is also roughly equivalent to Brazil’s annual CO2 emissions from fossil fuels.
The analysis accounts for the impact of the clean-tech exports in the destination country, as well as the emissions due to manufacturing the products in China.
Looking at the full-year data for 2025, manufacturing clean-energy equipment resulted in emissions of around 170MtCO2 within China, while avoiding 370MtCO2 in other countries. This implies that, in aggregate, it takes six months for the exported goods to pay back the CO2 from manufacturing.
Solar exports are the biggest enabler
China’s solar-equipment exports continue to be the biggest enabler of decarbonisation in other countries, according to the analysis.
In the full-year data for 2025, China exported finished solar panels and intermediate products that correspond to a total generating capacity of 436 gigawatts (GW) once assembled and installed.
(Note that this is measured in gigawatts DC, which reflects the capacity of the panels, whereas capacity measured in AC refers to the size of the wire that connects them to the grid.)
In addition, China exported 8GW of wind turbines. Together with the solar equipment, this will generate approximately 720 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity per year, based on the average output per unit of capacity for solar and wind in each destination country.
For 2026, China’s exports of wind and solar equipment are on track to generate approximately 800TWh of electricity, equivalent to the generation from around 100 coal-fired power plants.
Over their lifetimes, based on the power sources expected to be displaced in each destination country, the solar exports in 2025 will avoid an estimated 6,400MtCO2.
(For more details on the basis for these calculations, see: About the data.)
Solar is therefore the largest source of lifetime avoided CO2 emissions by far, with wind-turbine exports in second place displacing just 180MtCO2, as shown in the figure below.
The 39m electric vehicles exported from China in 2025 included 36m two-wheelers, 2.2m battery electric cars, 160,000 plug-in hybrid cars, 15,000 buses and 30,000 trucks.
In addition, China exported batteries with a capacity of 305 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025, enough to power another 5m battery electric cars once installed, based on typical battery sizes.
Based on typical driving distances and fuel consumption for corresponding fuel-burning vehicles, as well as the CO2 intensity of the electricity grid in destination countries, the EVs and batteries exported in 2025 will avoid an estimated 170MtCO2 over their lifetimes.
Given the sheer number of electric two-wheelers, the amount of oil and resulting CO2 they displace is a key uncertainty. Real–world e-bike studies support an assumption that roughly half of e-bike travel displaces the use of motor vehicles, either cars or motorbikes depending on location.
This suggests that, when taking into account the electricity grid in importing nations, China’s electric two-wheeler exports in 2025 will avoid an estimated 40MtCO2 over their lifetimes.
Global South dominates avoided emissions
In 2025, some 73% of the lifetime emissions avoided by China’s clean-tech exports were in global-south countries, which also accounted for 87% of the growth year-on-year.
In the first three quarters of 2026, global-south countries were responsible for almost all of the increase in avoided emissions compared with a year earlier, as shown in the figure below.
The high share of the global south in avoided emissions reflects large export volumes and power grids that are more carbon-intensive on average, as well as better average solar conditions that result in larger avoided emissions for each gigawatt of solar exported.
Clean-tech exports span the globe
On the regional level, South Asia has the largest avoided emissions due to imports of Chinese clean-tech, with strong year-on-year growth both in 2025 and the first three quarters of 2026.
Other top regional destinations in 2026 to date, in terms of lifetime avoided emissions, include south-east Asia, North America, Europe and the Middle East.
However, the exports span the globe, as shown in the map below, avoiding billions of tonnes of CO2 across every continent and in nearly every country of the world.
Among countries, the US has the second-largest avoided emissions after India. It registered a further increase of 12% in 2026, despite increased tariffs, and exceeds the EU as a bloc. The US is followed by Thailand, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Australia.
The EU imports more of every clean energy technology than the US, but the US has higher avoided emissions. This is because average US solar output per unit of capacity is higher – as is the average CO2 intensity of power generation. As a result, every gigawatt of solar installed in the US results in three-times more avoided CO2 emissions than in the EU.
The resilience of Chinese clean-tech exports to the US indicates strong demand for the technology, despite the Trump administration’s steps to slow down deployment and discourage imports.
The data suggests that reducing reliance on technology supply from China – a policy aim of recent administrations from both parties – is likely to require scaling up of domestic and third-country manufacturing of the key technologies, in order to meet that resilient demand.
The largest change in the national rankings for avoided emissions from clean-tech exports in 2026, compared with the previous year, has been a fall in exports to the Gulf countries affected by the war in the region.
For electric cars and heavy vehicles, western Europe was the largest destination in the first three quarters of 2026, followed by Latin America and south-east Asia, both of which more than doubled, reflecting the impact of the oil crisis. Exports to the EU gained 39%.
When including batteries and electric two-wheelers, North America and Europe are the largest destinations for avoided emissions due to EV-related exports, followed by Latin America and south-east Asia.
Exports of Chinese solar equipment to the US rose 13% year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026, once re-routing through different channels is considered. This is a reversal of the dip early in the year, due to a sharp increase in tariffs in June 2025. Exports of EVs and batteries to the US also increased slightly, by 3% in the first three quarters of 2026.
Overseas clean energy projects double over three years
In addition to its clean-tech exports, China is also increasingly becoming directly involved in the development of overseas clean-energy projects.
This can be traced back to the 2021 pledge by Chinese president Xi Jinping, in which he said:
“China will step up support for other developing countries in developing green and low-carbon energy, and will not build new coal-fired power projects abroad.”
As of July 2026, some 69GW of China-linked renewable energy projects were in operation overseas. An additional 100GW are being built, with 280GW in planning but not yet under construction. This renewable energy capacity is supported by 3.5GW of China-linked energy storage projects in operation, with a further 21.4GW of storage in the pipeline.
China has also financed and built six operating nuclear reactors overseas, with a total capacity of 3.3GW. These are all located in Pakistan and, in 2023, they had a total generation of 26TWh. China began construction on the 1.2GW Chashma-5 reactor in 2024, also in Pakistan, with the plant expected to be operational around 2030.
The expected electricity output of China’s newly operating overseas clean-power projects doubled from 2022 to 2025, with a further 6% year-on-year increase in the first seven months of 2026.
The countries with the largest estimated generation from China-linked clean-power capacity are Indonesia, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Mongolia, Zimbabwe, Laos, Turkey and South Africa.
The list looks slightly different when considering the impact of operating, under construction or planned China-linked capacity on avoided CO2 emissions.
As shown in the figure below, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan, Indonesia and Pakistan are expected to see the largest avoided CO2, once under-construction projects are completed.
The increase in overseas clean-energy projects has changed China’s role in the power-sector development of other emerging countries. Having previously been the main financier of coal-power projects, it is now an important force in developing clean-power generation.
Nevertheless, there are gaps in the implementation of Xi’s pledge to end overseas coal-power development, which could be seen to affect its effectiveness and credibility. These gaps are particularly with respect to “captive” coal-power plants linked to industrial projects in Indonesia.

indian-startups-bd7074d0a9.headline: Freshworks Acquires AI Startup Robusta To Strengthen IT Operations Platform
indian-startups-bd7074d0a9.fulltext: Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks has acquired Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev for an undisclosed amount to strengthen its IT service management platform Freshservice. The acquisition will add AI-powered capabilities to investigate technology outages, identify their underlying causes, and recommend corrective actions. Freshworks plans to integrate these capabilities into Freshservice and deepen their interoperability with incident response platforms such as FireHydrant. Founded by Natan Yellin and Arik Alon, Robusta uses AI agents to analyse monitoring data, information from IT infrastructure, and recent code or configuration changes to determine what caused an outage. It also identifies how disruptions affect connected services and recommends steps to resolve them. According to Freshworks, the technology is designed to reduce manual investigations, consolidate alerts, and help engineering teams resolve incidents faster. Engineers can review and approve recommended actions before changes are made to production systems. “Our technology lets AI Agents do that effectively in large enterprise environments, where there are so many raw events that investigating each one individually would be exorbitant from a token cost perspective. We're incredibly excited to join Freshworks, which gives us the scale and platform to bring that experience to engineering teams everywhere, while keeping humans firmly in control of decisions that touch production,” said Robusta founder Yellin. Freshworks said the integration would connect incident diagnosis, response, and prevention workflows, helping businesses use findings from earlier outages to reduce recurring disruptions. The deal expands Freshworks’ AI-powered service operations offerings, which focus on automating IT workflows and helping enterprises manage technology incidents. Founded in 2010 by Girish Mathrubootham and Shanmugam Krishnasamy, Freshworks offers cloud-based software for customer engagement, sales, and IT service management. The Robusta deal follows Freshworks’ agreement to acquire Torii, announced earlier this month. The SaaS management platform helps enterprises track software usage and govern AI spending. The company also acquired US-based incident management startup FireHydrant in Demember last year. While FireHydrant helps enterprises coordinate responses to software outages, Robusta adds AI-powered root-cause analysis and remediation recommendations. On the financial front, Freshworks reported a $4.8 Mn net loss for Q1 2026, even as revenue grew 16% YoY to $228.6 Mn. It also announced plans to cut around 11% of its workforce, or approximately 500 employees, as it sought to increase the use of AI in product development and automate routine work.

indian-startups-b06106be81.headline: Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups
indian-startups-b06106be81.fulltext:
Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning.
U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done.
Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase. Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020.
Size your seed against the Series A
Uncork Capital‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal.
A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic, a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed, right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures, then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later.
Map your Series A leads now
Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything.
Sell your way to the bar
The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion.
At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine.
From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside.
A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one.

india-deep-tech-1c5628c5ca.headline: Why India Needs To ‘Smell The Coffee’ On Future Warfare
india-deep-tech-1c5628c5ca.fulltext:
When General David Petraeus, former Director of the CIA and commander of US forces in Iraq and Afghanistan, delivered his prescription for modern warfare at the NDTV World Summit last week, it reverberated sharply through India’s national security corridors. His message was stark: future battlefields will be dominated by drone swarms, cheap autonomous weapons, and algorithmic warfare where traditional maneuver assets like tanks, surface ships, and manned aircraft face extreme vulnerability. In Petraeus’s view, every military on Earth requires a top-to-bottom institutional revolution, unlearning legacy concepts, overhaul of procurement cycles to weekly software iterations, and turning force structures on their heads.
However, when applied to India, a country that only recently nearly went to war with one nuclear neighbour, has an ongoing military standoff with another, how realistic is this radical prescription?
On NDTV’s India Matters, anchored by LivefistDefence.com founder Shiv Aroor, former Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Arun Prakash, a 1971 war hero and naval aviator now a strategic affairs commentator, delivered a sobering, unvarnished reality check from the perspective of India’s military establishment. While acknowledging Petraeus’s insights into Ukraine and the Middle East, Admiral Prakash outlined why India remains dangerously far from executing such a transformation, constrained by structural inertia, political distraction, and a widening technological gap with China.
General Petraeus urged militaries to throw out legacy playbooks and embrace rapid institutional change. But as Admiral Prakash pointed out, the Indian defence ecosystem historically struggles with even routine administrative shifts, making a revolutionary leap nearly unthinkable under current conditions.
“Executing a revolution is not something easy especially in military affairs where… we are very conservative and unfortunately in India even routine issues take years and decades to implement so bringing about a revolution is… a little out of our reach.”
To underline the point, Admiral Prakash highlighted India’s agonisingly sluggish pace of structural reform:
“To take ordinary decisions like reorganizing our 17 commands into theaters has taken 6 years after the government gave an express order directive to the newly minted Chief of Defence Staff… We need to go well back in 2001 when the group of ministers following the Kargil episode directed the constitution of the Strategic Forces Command and the Andaman Nicobar Command—those were the first baby steps towards jointness, but 25 years have passed.”
The root cause, according to the former Navy Chief, lies in a fundamental disconnect at the top of the decision-making pyramid.
“…These things need to originate at the political level… My feeling is that the political establishment is far too much involved in politics and not enough in national security.”
The rapid evolution of unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and loitering munitions in ongoing global conflicts has already altered naval and aerial warfare dynamics, a key point made by Gen Petraeus. Admiral Prakash highlighted how non-state actors and nations without conventional navies are inflicting asymmetric damage on major powers:
“If you look at Ukraine, the country doesn’t have a navy to speak of but they’ve decimated the Russian navy… sank their flagship the Moskva… The Russian Navy is clinging to the east coast of the Black Sea… If you look at Iran, their air force has been decimated by the Americans and the Israelis, and yet they’ve got the Americans on the run—they’ve rained missiles and drones on 14 US bases in West Asia. Tanks and infantry are rarely seen on the Ukrainian battlefield… all these are factors which lead to what we are calling a revolution.”
India stands on the verge of allocating tens of billions of dollars toward heavy capital platforms, including potentially a third aircraft carrier, conventional and nuclear submarines, and 114 Rafale fighters. Admiral Prakash questioned whether committing scarce capital to long-gestation legacy platforms makes sense when the global balance is shifting toward algorithmic warfare.
“We are on the cusp of spending a great deal of money on weapon platform acquisitions whether it’s an aircraft carrier, submarines, or fighter aircraft… Projects like AMCA are about 10 to 15 years from realization. Should we be spending money on these kinds of platforms, or should we switch now and put money into artificial intelligence, algorithmic warfare?”
Comparing India’s technological readiness with Western developments reveals a stark gap:
“The Maven Smart System project was kicked off by the US armed forces… 10 years ago… Today they have something called the Maven Smart System. We don’t even have a large language model. We don’t even have a search engine which we can call Indian.”
Given the time required to build true indigenous technological depth, Admiral Prakash offered a grim tactical assessment:
“If we are going to try to catch up with China, then we need a spell of peace. Therefore, our politicians, our statesmen, and our diplomats need to ensure that we have a 10 to 15-year period of peace… which will allow us the breathing spell to catch up.”
General Petraeus asserted that the human is no longer “in the loop,” but rather “on the loop”, supervising systems that execute targeting at machine speed. Admiral Prakash cautioned against removing human moral judgment from lethal kill chains, citing ethical failures already visible in contemporary combat:
“…Theoretically speaking, it’ll be a sad day if the human being is taken out of the loop because AI is already galloping… There has to be a human being in the loop to exercise ethical caution and precaution… No matter how advanced the systems get, military ethics demands that we keep a man in the loop so the final trigger or the firing button is pressed at the behest of a human being…”
A core theme of Admiral Prakash’s critique was India’s tendency to create national security catchphrases that obscure a lack of concrete capability on the ground.
“We have conclaves, samvads, and seminars… but really are issues of contention subjected to debate and thrown about?… We need to catch the bull by the horns and realize how far astern, how far back we have been left behind. Examples of things like integrated battle groups, Cold Start, preferred security partner, etc.—those all turned into slogans; nothing happened after they were mouthed.”
He singled out critical technology bottlenecks, such as the decades-long struggle to develop an indigenous jet engine:
“Issues like the Kaveri engine… unless we have an aero-engine, our aerospace industry, we can bid goodbye to it… and there again, it’s a lack of political will, lack of funding, lack of intervention at the right point.”
He warned that entering a conflict without addressing these core deficiencies risks severe consequences:
“I think we are chasing too many mirages and issues which are not really of substance. So we need to come down to earth, face the reality, smell the coffee of what’s going to happen tomorrow, and either we gird our loins and tackle the problems, put money where our mouths are… If we go into a conflict with our present organization of 17 commands scattered all over the country and our archaic system of doing things… I don’t see a very happy future.”
The most glaring contrast, according to both Gen Petraeus and Admiral Prakash, in military planning across the Line of Actual Control (LAC) lies in China’s disciplined, step-by-step execution. While Beijing formulates regular Defence White Papers and builds vast industrial capacity, India still lacks a published National Security Strategy.
“China is very clear-eyed and resolute about where it stands… They produce a defence white paper every two years… You can make out what a clear-eyed vision they have… We have even denied the need for a national security strategy. So if we don’t know where we are going, how will we get there at all?”
The disparity in industrial manufacturing capacity is equally striking:
“China’s shipbuilding capacity is about… 20 times that of the USA. They can churn out an aircraft carrier in two to three years, we took 16 years. They’re pushing out destroyers and frigates in matters of weeks and months…”
Admiral Prakash concluded with a call for self-examination, warning against taking refuge in economic headline numbers or grand political slogans:
“We’ve declared ourselves a Vishwaguru already, but technologically we are ages behind China… We repeat ad nauseam that we are the third largest or fourth largest economy in the world. I don’t think that matters, it is the per capita GDP that is going to matter… So I think we need to smell the coffee, keep in touch with reality, especially where national security is concerned.”
General David Petraeus’s vision of future warfare provides an important benchmark for modern militaries. However, Admiral Arun Prakash’s intervention serves as a necessary, sobering reality check. High-concept military theories cannot substitute for clear national security strategy, sustained R&D funding, political focus, and streamlined procurement. Until India moves past slogans and addresses these foundational gaps, adapting to the future of warfare will remain an uphill climb.

global-economics-7995ecec87.headline: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
global-economics-7995ecec87.fulltext:
DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals “as a precaution” while it investigated the situation and engaged with law enforcement.
The company added that user funds were safe.
The price of Bitcoin fell about 5 percent following the incident, dropping below $77,000.
“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said the exchange appeared to have been targeted in a cyber heist.
“It does look like a hack on Binance,” Zhao, who no longer manages Binance’s operation after stepping down as CEO in 2023, said in a post on X.
“I don’t manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
If confirmed, the hacking could rank as the largest theft of crypto assets in history, exceeding the $1.5bn crypto heist carried out by the North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group in 2025.
Cyber criminals stolen $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by market intelligence firm TRM.

global-economics-88a60165c4.headline: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%
global-economics-88a60165c4.fulltext:
The European Central Bank voted to hold interest rates steady on Thursday, meeting market expectations, despite euro zone inflation rising to a three-year high.
It keeps the central bank's key rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5% following a 25 basis point hike in September.
In a statement, the institution's Governing Council said rising energy prices posed upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to growth, but that underlying inflation and wages were so far broadly stable.
"At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach during a press conference.
Lagarde identified the main developments since the ECB's last meeting as higher energy costs across oil, petrol, fuel, gas and refining margins, and a sharp rise in long-term financing costs, with the average 10-year sovereign yield up by around 35 basis points.
"If you combine these two factors — actually, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate — but on the basis of the uncertainty that accumulates and that rises as well, on the basis of underlying inflation that has broadly remained unchanged, the Governing Council unanimously decided that we were well positioned enough at this stage to hold and that a measured approach at this point in time remained appropriate," Lagarde said.
Money markets were pricing in around a 67% probability of a rate hike in December following the announcement, according to LSEG data.
Headline inflation in the euro area hit 3.8% last month, the highest level since September 2023. Energy price inflation reached 18.8% amid continued turbulence in the Middle East.
The resurgence in energy price pressures following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February saw the ECB hike rates in June for the first time since 2023.
The euro area economy continued to expand in the third quarter of the year, with a recovery in services since the start of the Middle East conflict, the Governing Council said in an explanation of its decision Thursday.
Manufacturing, digital services and exports are being boosted by AI-related investments, while government spending on infrastructure and defense is supporting business activity. However, energy price pressures are likely to hit consumer confidence as higher financing costs weigh on growth.
In her press conference, Lagarde said the ECB would continue monitoring rising French borrowing costs and increased fragmentation that has spooked some market watchers.
Lagarde noted borrowing costs at the long end of the curve were rising significantly around the world, which she attributed to expectations for inflation and interest rates as well as "debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers," which she said were issuing more long-term bonds and driving up competition.
One more hike?
"Predicting the path of ECB monetary policy is becoming more challenging," Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said in a note on Thursday.
"One question is whether the two hikes already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September are enough to lean against the further increase in energy inflation risk? Probably not."
Wall said the other main question was whether the looming departure of Lagarde as ECB president — a decision she announced earlier on Thursday — would impact decision-making next year.
"We think the institution is bigger than the person, but there's uncertainty. We expect one more hike to 2.75% in December while Lagarde is still President, and that's probably the end of the hiking cycle."
Dean Turner, chief euro zone and U.K. economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, said the Thursday decision "should be viewed as a hawkish pause rather than the end of the tightening cycle."
France's fiscal challenge is not expected to change the direction of monetary policy "in the absence of broader financial stress," he said in emailed comments.
"The ECB's focus remains firmly on ensuring that today's energy-driven inflation does not develop into a more persistent problem."

global-economics-a22613dfbb.headline: President Christine Lagarde to leave European Central Bank in February 2027

President Christine Lagarde announced she’ll leave the European Central Bank in early 2027, intensifying the struggle to replace one of the world’s most powerful monetary policymakers.

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos and the Netherlands’ Klaas Knot are vying for Lagarde’s job. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October reckon De Cos, a former Bank of Spain chief who currently heads the Bank for International Settlements, is favorite.

global-economics-d46195ac62.fulltext:
Frankfurt [Germany], October 30 (ANI): European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde on Thursday informed the Governing Council and European Council President Antonio Costa that she would step down from her position on February 7, 2027.
Her successor will be appointed by the European Council following the nomination process set out in Article 283 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, according to a press statement issued by the bank.
The Governing Council thanked President Lagarde warmly and presented her with a sustained ovation, the statement said.
"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde said in a video statement posted on social media.
Lagarde is departing seven months before the formal expiry of her term. European Council President Costa stated that the process to identify her successor would start without delay.
The vacancy is set to be filled in tandem with other senior ECB roles becoming available. These include the executive board seat of Isabel Schnabel, who will depart in early January, and the post of chief economist Philip Lane, who will leave in May.
Former central bank governors from the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely regarded as the principal contenders to succeed Lagarde as head of the European Central Bank.
Lagarde has chosen to leave office as her home country, France, approaches elections. She has confirmed that she will not stand for the French presidency but will continue to champion pro-European values in France "in whichever capacity" she judges most effective.
Lagarde, 70, previously served as French finance minister and led the International Monetary Fund. (ANI)

world-70cae7a87b.headline: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result
world-70cae7a87b.fulltext:
More than half of Victoria’s lawyers have reported using AI in their work, according to a new study, but just over a quarter say they have reduced fees as a result of efficiency gains.
They also say clients seeking advice from chatbots have added to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.
The 2026 census of 2,221 of the state’s lawyers, conducted by the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner’s legal services research centre, found a big increase in lawyers using AI in their practices, rising from 37% to 55% in the last year.
While the 2025 report found AI use was highest among those under 30 years of age, in 2026 this disparity had largely disappeared, although usage remained low for those aged 60 and over.
AI use was most common in trade practices (85%), banking and finance (78%) and information technology and telecommunications (78%), while it was used much less in criminal law (29%), family law (45%) and administrative law (46%).
While there are AI tools designed specifically for legal services, 79% of lawyers reported using consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot. Legal-specific tools alone were used by 22% of respondents.
The increased use in AI has not translated to a reduction in fees for most, the survey found, with just 26% of lawyers responding that their use of AI had resulted in lower client fees.
Reduced fees were more likely to be reported by those working for business clients (34%) compared with individual fee-paying clients (23%).
Some reported AI had enabled them to take on work that would have previously been uneconomical (18%).
The principal researcher and report co-author, Dr Georgie Rychner, said fee reductions in corporate and big firms could be attributed to the fact clients in those settings were repeat users of legal services.
“They have a high level of legal capability,” she said. “They also are perhaps using AI in their own work, so they have a better understanding and are able to advocate for lower prices … whereas we’re not seeing that as much in the community legal system sector.”
Rychner said the efficiency gains of using AI were not as high as expected, but that in 2025 the survey found 89% of practitioners said they had taken steps to verify the accuracy of AI output, which might have negated the gains.
In 2026 there had been a rise in clients using AI for their own legal research, she said, with 46% of lawyers reporting their clients were arriving with inaccurate or misleading information, and 41% presenting AI-generated documents that required correction.
Nearly half of lawyers said there was an increase in time and effort required if their clients used AI, compared with 19% who said it led to a reduction in time and effort.
“What we are hearing is that clients are more frequently arriving with misleading or inaccurate information about their legal problems, more so than they’re arriving with a better understanding of legal problems,” she said, adding that more research was needed to understand client perspectives.
Courts and legal practitioner bodies across Australia have been grappling with the rise in AI use among lawyers and the public since 2023.
A Victorian lawyer last year was the first in the country to face sanctions for false citations discovered, being stripped of his ability to practise as a principal lawyer. Investigations were also launched by regulatory bodies in Western Australia and New South Wales in similar cases.
The federal court in April issued new rules around using generative AI, while the chief justice of the high court, Stephen Gageler, said last year the use of AI-generated content in legal cases had reached an “unsustainable phase”.

DoorDash announced Thursday that it will buy rival Instacart for $17 billion in a deal that the company says will help local businesses compete with delivery giants such as Amazon and Walmart.
One of the most popular app-based delivery services in the U.S., DoorDash delivers hot meals from restaurants as well as groceries and other items from stores including CVS and Target. The company is paying $65 per share in cash and stock to acquire Instacart, which represents a 26% premium to Instacart's closing stock before the first media reports of the planned acquisition.
Instacart occupies a narrower niche than its soon-to-be owner — it offers grocery delivery from supermarkets and some retailers but does not deliver prepared meals. It went public in 2023 after experiencing a surge in demand related to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The combination of the two San Francisco-based rivals has already raised antitrust concerns, but it could also help combat the dominance of major e-commerce companies.
"The tie-up between these two companies could create a little more monopolistic power," said Scott Hanson, a financial advisor and co-founder of Allworth Financial. "But on the other hand, maybe it gives them an opportunity to compete more head-on with Amazon."
The deal could also help DoorDash build on its expansion into grocery delivery, analysts said, and give the company a financial boost after seeing its shares fall 20% so far this year. DoorDash shares were up 3% on Thursday after its announcement, reaching $177.62 per share with a market value of $75 billion.
Instacart shares have risen 30% this year and fell nearly 2% in midday trading Thursday to above $57 per share. Its market value sat around $13 billion.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash co-founder and Chief Executive Tony Xu said in a statement. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools."

global-economics-9d409941a1.fulltext:
A KsheerasagarPublished29 Oct 2026, 07:05 PM IST Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has announced a change to the US central bank’s meeting schedule, with the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) planning to dedicate one of its eight meetings in 2027 exclusively to discussions on monetary policy strategy, without a vote on interest rates or an accompanying policy statement. Warsh said the revised schedule would take effect next autumn, with the Fed maintaining eight meetings annually but placing greater emphasis on longer-term strategic discussions alongside its regular interest-rate decisions. The change is expected to evolve further in 2028, when Warsh expects two meetings to be dedicated to strategy discussions and the remaining six to monetary policy decisions. “We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC,” Warsh said, explaining that the revised schedule would allow policymakers to balance their assessment of near-term economic developments with broader discussions on the direction of monetary policy. He said that while regular meetings are necessary to assess incoming economic data, the central bank also needs time to examine major policy questions over longer horizons. “I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail. It's an institutional choice affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and ultimately the wisdom of our decisions,” Warsh said. The announcement comes as the Fed continues to work towards its 2% inflation target, with questions remaining over whether monetary policy should be tightened further. Asked why the Fed had not raised interest rates despite limited progress towards its inflation target and a relatively stable labour market, Warsh said price stability could not be judged by a single date on the calendar or an isolated economic data point. “Ensuring price stability, quashing inflation, is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar. Same way, it's not about some isolated data point,” he said. Warsh added that the Fed had reinforced its commitment to the 2% inflation target, taken responsibility for delivering price stability, and outlined its monetary policy framework. He also pointed to the Fed’s September decision to remove some monetary policy accommodation as part of its efforts to bring inflation under control. Warsh said measures of inflation compensation and inflation expectations were moving in the right direction, although he acknowledged that the global environment remained unsettled. “I’m encouraged by the progress we’ve made in a short period of time,” he said, while acknowledging that the Fed had not yet achieved price stability. He added that policymakers would use the coming period to assess incoming information and determine the appropriate course of action to deliver on the central bank’s inflation objective. The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25 percentage point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term 2 per cent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.
US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fuelled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies.
Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the buildout of huge data centres to support it.
The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump’s Republicans.
Trump’s handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
US consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7 per cent, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed – including Warsh – have signalled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.
Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, Warsh said that US economic conditions had “broadly conformed” to policymakers’ expectations, fuelling speculation that the Fed may pause at the October meeting.
On Wednesday, the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.
Wendy Edelberg, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said before the meeting that a decision to hold after raising rates in September was potentially contradictory, given the labour market – the Fed’s other mandate – has been largely stable.
“In terms of the economics of it, I don’t totally understand the logic,” she said.
“If there was a reason to raise interest rates at the last meeting, I think that there’s just as compelling of an economic reason to raise interest rates at this meeting.”
The Fed has a dual mandate to maintain maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term target.
It achieves this goal largely using one tool: the economy’s key interest rate. Raising rates tends to cool inflation but can also dampen economic activity; lowering them can spur economic activity but also fuel inflation.
The US unemployment rate has been largely stable around 4.2 per cent over the last year, with job growth mostly in positive territory – albeit driven by a few sectors.
Other advanced economies have also been grappling with high inflation, and on Wednesday Canada’s central bank raised its key rate to 2.5 per cent, its first hike since July 2023.
Loretta Mester, former head of the Cleveland Fed, took part in FOMC meetings during her tenure and insisted that the committee did not “take into account any kind of political issues” when it debated monetary policy.
Still, Trump has loomed large over the Fed since he returned to power last year.
In his second term, he has led an unprecedented assault on the Fed’s independence, pursuing criminal charges against Warsh’s predecessor Jerome Powell and attempting to fire Governor Cook as he demanded lower interest rates.
While the probe against Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh’s Senate confirmation, the White House has recently renewed its drive to fire Cook – despite a Supreme Court decision that batted back an earlier attempt.
“I don’t think it’s going to stop because I think it’s in the nature of this administration to continue those attacks,” Mester said.

india-bc3b559938.headline: India's economy estimated to grow 7.35% in July-September quarter: Finance Ministry
india-bc3b559938.fulltext:
New Delhi [India], October 29 (ANI): India's economy is estimated to have grown by 7.35 per cent in the July-September quarter of the current financial year (FY27), supported by strong domestic demand, industrial activity and higher consumption, according to the Finance Ministry's October Monthly Economic Review.
The estimate, based on the ministry's nowcasting model, comes after the economy recorded growth of 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter. The ministry had earlier projected growth of around 7.3 per cent for the second quarter in its September review.
"Following real GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1 FY27, the Department's nowcasting model, introduced in the Economic Survey 2025-26, nowcasts real GDP growth of 7.35 per cent in Q2 FY27," the report stated.
The review highlighted that several key economic indicators, including industrial production, electricity consumption, port traffic, GST collections and automobile sales, recorded stronger growth during the second quarter.
"Taken together, these indicators point to sustained growth momentum in Q2 FY27," it said.
Gross GST collections grew by around 15 per cent during the July-September quarter, compared with approximately 8.4 per cent in the preceding quarter. Domestic automobile sales also increased by around 25 per cent year-on-year, supported by demand across rural and urban markets.
The report noted that business activity showed signs of improvement towards the end of the quarter, with manufacturing and services activity strengthening in September.
"The recovery in PMI readings, alongside improved business sentiment, points to a cautiously favourable outlook for the coming months," it said.
On the outlook for the remainder of FY27, the ministry said domestic consumption, investment activity and structural reforms were expected to support economic growth.
"Healthy credit growth and recent trade agreements are expected to provide additional support to consumption, investment and exports," the review stated.
However, the ministry cautioned that global uncertainties, including higher crude oil prices, geopolitical tensions and inflationary pressures, could continue to pose challenges.
"Overall, while persistent geopolitical frictions, energy price volatility and global financial tightening remain key headwinds, the Indian economy may remain well-positioned to sustain its expansionary trajectory through the rest of FY27," the report said.
The International Monetary Fund has projected India's economy to grow by 7.0 per cent in FY27, while the World Bank, OECD and Reserve Bank of India have forecast growth of 7.1 per cent. (ANI)

india-c858c664b6.fulltext:

NEW DELHI: Commerce minister 
Piyush Goyal
 on Saturday assured that the India-US trade deal framework will not harm Indian farmers, MSMEs, artisans, or craftsmen, and said their interests remain fully protected.
"I can say with absolute certainty that the farmers, MSMEs, artisans, and craftsmen of India will not suffer any kind of loss," Goyal said in a press conference.
He said the agreement will instead help Indian farmers by opening the US market to their products. "Agricultural products from Indian farmers will be exported to the United States at zero duty. At the same time, no tariff concessions have been granted for agricultural products from US farmers entering the Indian market," he said.
Goyal said the deal improves conditions for Indian exporters. "The 50% reciprocal tariff has been reduced to 18% which is less compared to our neighbouring countries, and will provide a lot of help to our exporters. The deal brings new hopes and opportunities in India's growth story," he said.
The commerce minister stressed that Indian producers will gain more access to the US market. "I can state categorically and without any hesitation that India's farmers, MSMEs, artisans, and craftsmen will not suffer any loss. 
On the contrary, India will benefit from greater access to the US market," he said.
The minister said the agreement will boost employment and support labour-intensive sectors. "It is a big thrust to MSMEs employing a large number of women and youth. With exports from labour intensive sectors like textiles & apparel, leather & footwear, toys, and gems & jewellery to the US set to scale, lakhs of jobs will be created while boosting domestic manufacturing," he added.
He said tariffs will go down to zero on several key Indian export sectors. "Additionally, tariffs will go down to zero on a wide range of goods, including generic pharmaceuticals, gems & diamonds, and aircraft parts, thereby further enhancing India's export competitiveness and Make in India," Goyal said.
He added that several agricultural and food products will also benefit. "These also include spices, tea, coffee, coconut oil, cashew nuts, and several fruits and vegetables such as avocado, banana, mango, pineapple, and mushrooms, along with select bakery products," he said.
